"Bad faith" means deliberate insincerity — acting as though you mean something when you don't, or pretending to engage honestly while secretly working against that very engagement.

The key word is deliberate. Bad faith is never an accident. It's a conscious choice to deceive, mislead, or pretend. This is what separates it from a simple mistake, misunderstanding, or failure.

Think of it this way: if you promise a friend you'll help them move, but you never planned to show up — you just said it to avoid awkward conflict — that's bad faith. You made a commitment with no intention of keeping it.

The term comes from the Latin phrase "mala fides" (bad faith), as opposed to "bona fides" (good faith). This Latin origin is why you'll often hear its opposite — bona fide — used in English to mean "genuine" or "authentic" (e.g., "a bona fide expert").

Good faith is the foundation of all honest human interaction: the silent agreement that when we make promises, argue positions, or enter agreements, we mean what we say. Bad faith is the violation of that foundation.

In ordinary conversation and social situations, bad faith means going through the motions of honest engagement while your actual intent is hidden and contradicts those motions.

Some clear examples:

The fake consultation. A manager calls a team meeting to "gather everyone's ideas" before making a decision, but the decision has already been made. The consultation is theater. That's bad faith — because the form of honest engagement (asking for input) is being used while the substance of it (actually considering the input) is absent.

The insincere apology. Someone says "I'm sorry" not because they regret anything, but because saying it gets them out of trouble. The words are there; the meaning isn't.

The stall tactic. A person keeps asking you for "more information" in a debate, not because they genuinely want to understand, but because they have no intention of ever updating their position and are using questions as a delay strategy. They're mimicking open-mindedness while being closed.

In all of these cases, the form of good-faith behavior is present (the meeting, the apology, the questions), but the substance is absent. This gap between appearance and intent is the hallmark of bad faith.
Bad Faith in Philosophy (The Deepest Version)

The philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre gave "bad faith" its most profound and precise meaning. In his existentialist philosophy, bad faith (mauvaise foi in French) means lying to yourself about your own freedom.

Here's his insight: human beings are fundamentally free. We always have choices, even when those choices are difficult or painful. Bad faith is when a person pretends they have no choice — when they deny their own freedom in order to escape the anxiety and responsibility that comes with it.

Sartre's famous example: The waiter. Sartre describes a waiter who performs his role with exaggerated precision — every gesture, every posture, every movement is perfectly waiter-like. He seems to be trying to become a waiter in the way a stone is a stone — as though he has no identity beyond the role, no choices outside the job. Sartre says this waiter is in bad faith. He's pretending he has no freedom, that he is simply and entirely "a waiter," to avoid confronting the uncomfortable truth that he chooses to be there, could choose to leave, and must take responsibility for that choice.

Another example: Someone who says "I had no choice" when they clearly did have a choice — they just found the alternatives unpleasant. Saying "I had to lie to my boss or I would've been fired" is different from "I simply had no choice." You had a choice; you made a calculation. Denying that is bad faith toward yourself.

Why this matters philosophically: Sartre argued that bad faith is one of the most common and destructive things humans do. By pretending we are defined by our roles, our past, our circumstances, or society's expectations — rather than by our free choices — we escape responsibility. We become passive objects rather than active agents of our own lives. For Sartre, living authentically means acknowledging your freedom and owning your choices, even when that's terrifying.

This philosophical sense of bad faith is self-deception, while the everyday sense is deception of others. But both share the same core structure: a knowing, deliberate pretense about what is real.

Law is where bad faith becomes the most precisely defined, and where the stakes are often the highest. Legal systems across the world are built on the principle that parties in any agreement must act in "good faith and fair dealing." Bad faith is the violation of this legal duty.

Crucially: In law, bad faith is not merely being wrong, being careless, or making a bad deal. It requires intentional dishonest or deceptive conduct. Negligence (failing through carelessness) is different from bad faith (acting through deliberate wrongdoing).

In Contract Law

When two parties sign a contract, most legal systems assume — even without writing it down — that both sides will deal with each other honestly and fairly. This is called the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.

Bad faith in contracts means one party is working to undermine the purpose of the agreement while technically appearing to comply. For example: a company hires a salesperson and promises a commission on any deal they bring in. Then, every time the salesperson is about to close a deal, the company quietly sabotages it to avoid paying the commission. The company hasn't technically broken a written rule — but it has acted in bad faith by betraying the spirit and purpose of the agreement.

In Insurance Law

This is one of the most developed areas of bad faith law. When you pay insurance premiums, the insurer takes on a duty to handle your claims honestly and fairly. Insurance bad faith occurs when an insurer:

  • Denies a valid claim without a legitimate reason
  • Delays payment unreasonably to pressure the claimant into accepting less
  • Fails to properly investigate a claim
  • Misrepresents the terms of the policy to avoid paying

Because insurance companies hold enormous power over policyholders (who are often in vulnerable situations — after an accident, a fire, a medical crisis), courts treat insurance bad faith especially seriously. In many places, it is a separate legal offense that can result in extra damages being awarded against the insurer.

In Negotiations

When two parties sit down to negotiate — whether it's a business deal, a labor contract, or a peace treaty — there's an expectation that both sides are genuinely trying to reach an agreement. Bad faith negotiation is when one side enters the process with no real intention of reaching an agreement, but uses the negotiation to gather information, stall for time, or create the appearance of trying while actually pursuing a hidden agenda.

In labor law, this is highly regulated. Employers and unions are legally required to "bargain in good faith" with each other. A tactic called surface bargaining — where a party goes through all the motions of negotiation (showing up, listening, making proposals) but has privately decided never to agree to anything — is considered bad faith negotiation and is illegal in many jurisdictions.

In Litigation (Legal Proceedings)

Lawyers and parties in a lawsuit also have good faith obligations. Filing a lawsuit you know is completely baseless, just to harass someone or drain their resources, is considered bad faith litigation. Courts can penalize this behavior by ordering the bad-faith party to pay the other side's legal fees.
Bad Faith in Diplomacy and International Relations

Nations that sign treaties are expected to honor them in good faith. This principle is even enshrined in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, which states that treaties must be performed in good faith (pacta sunt servanda — "agreements must be kept").

When a country signs a peace deal, trade agreement, or arms limitation treaty while privately planning to violate it from the start, that is bad faith at the international level. It's particularly serious because global trust and cooperation depend on nations meaning what they say in formal agreements.

The single most important thing about bad faith is that it requires intent. This is what makes it different from:

ConceptExplanation

Bad faith vs. mistake: If a builder constructs a wall that cracks because he misjudged the soil, that's a mistake — perhaps even negligence. If he builds a wall he knows is structurally unsound and tells the client it's fine, that's bad faith. The difference is knowledge and intent.

Bad faith vs. incompetence: A doctor who prescribes the wrong treatment because of limited knowledge is incompetent (and possibly negligent). A doctor who prescribes an unnecessary treatment knowing it won't help, just to collect fees, is acting in bad faith.

Bad faith vs. changed mind: If you sincerely intend to fulfill a promise but later decide not to, that may be a breach of trust — but it started in good faith. Bad faith means the deceptive intent was there from the beginning, or that you made no genuine effort to fulfill your obligation.

Here are the telltale patterns:

Hidden motives. The person's stated reason for doing something is different from their actual reason. They say they're asking for your feedback but really they want to look consultative to their boss.

Going through the motions. They perform the ritual of engagement — having the meeting, writing the letter, making the offer — without genuine commitment to what that ritual represents.

The pre-decided outcome. They appear open to discussion, but the conclusion is fixed before the conversation begins. The discussion is theater.

Exploiting the process. They use the formal mechanisms of good-faith interaction (negotiation, appeal, consultation) not to reach their stated goal but to achieve something else entirely — delay, information gathering, reputation management.

Consistency between words and actions. Bad faith often reveals itself over time because actions eventually contradict stated intentions. Someone who repeatedly fails to fulfill promises they made enthusiastically — especially when each failure benefits them — is likely acting in bad faith.
Why "Bad Faith" Is a Powerful Concept

Calling something "bad faith" is a strong accusation precisely because it targets intent, not just outcome. It says: you weren't confused, you weren't trying and failing — you were pretending. This is why bad faith is taken so seriously in law, philosophy, and ethics.

In practical terms, bad faith corrodes trust. Trust is built on the reasonable expectation that people mean what they say and say what they mean. When bad faith enters the picture, that foundation collapses. Agreements become unreliable, negotiations become pointless, and relationships — personal, professional, or political — break down.

Bad faith = deliberate insincerity. You are pretending to engage honestly while your real intent is something else entirely.

It appears in three main areas:

  • Everyday life: Fake consultations, insincere apologies, sham agreements.
  • Philosophy (Sartre): Lying to yourself that you have no freedom or choice to escape responsibility.
  • Law: Dishonestly undermining agreements, insurance claims, negotiations, or court proceedings.

The defining feature is always intent. Bad faith is never an accident. It is the knowing gap between what you appear to be doing and what you are actually doing.
